title: It's the Screens, Stupid
author: Alexander Thompson
summary: Thompson reviews James Marriott's The New Dark Ages and finds it frustrating not because the worry about post-literacy is silly but because the book fires eight loosely related arguments at once and calls the result a thesis. He separates the claims, ranging from cultural simplification and lost agency to cognitive decline and the end of democracy, and objects that the whole becomes a media theory of everything in which smartphones explain both PISA results and populist politics. His substantive reply is empirical. On IQ he grants the Reverse Flynn Effect but points out the cable television study Marriott leans on yields roughly 1.4 points over eighteen years and accounts for about twelve percent of the observed fall. On PISA he notes that US reading scores rose after 2012, that England and Estonia held steady after 2015 while neighbours declined, and that Singapore, Taiwan and Japan avoided decline altogether, which no screen-diffusion account explains. His alternative is that a country's education system matters more than its television, with knowledge-rich curricula, direct instruction and systematic phonics doing the work. The review ends on a diagnosis of tone: Marriott defends readers while flinching from any claim that some readers are more sophisticated than others.
points: Breaks the book's argument into eight separate claims and shows they are asserted together rather than connected, producing a media theory of everything.
Reexamines the central IQ evidence, noting the Norwegian cable television study implies about 1.4 points across eighteen years and explains roughly twelve percent of the measured decline.
Uses cross-national PISA patterns as the decisive test, since American, English and East Asian trajectories diverge in ways screen adoption cannot account for.
Proposes education systems as the better explanatory variable, crediting knowledge-rich curricula, direct instruction and systematic phonics in Estonia and England.
Identifies the book's unresolved tension, that it treats post-literacy as a threat to the enlightenment while refusing any claim of cultural or intellectual hierarchy.
quotes: Marriott argues that screens - specifically, television, cable TV, the internet, and social media - are coaxing us into a world without books. Without books, we are becoming post-literate.
Post-literacy is different from illiteracy. We can still read, but we prefer videos and podcasts to writing. This laziness is transforming us from a written society into an oral society.

What we get is a “media theory of everything”, where smartphones (and television) are roped in to explain everything from Bukele to PISA score decline. This is reckless and unhelpful: even though I agree with some of the points, it is hard to disentangle what is real versus what is projection.
This study, however, shows small effect sizes – approximately 1.4 IQ points for 18 years of television, which the authors admit explains about 12% of the measured fall during this time.

Why did England and Scotland fall so precipitously from 2000 to 2005 whilst America improved? Why did England and Estonia hold steady after 2015 whilst most other OECD countries declined? How have Singapore, Taiwan, Japan avoided decline altogether?
A better explanation is that a country’s education system is more important than its television diffusion.
James Marriott believes post-literacy endangers democracy - perhaps even the enlightenment itself. But he also cringes from any kind of intellectual elitism beyond ‘Tiktok is bad”.
Marriott and the other champions of readers are like environmentalists ashamed of defending trees.
